fixed: v2, on Biku's word (2026-10-16: 'there are multiple frames where there is no information or little information shown'): every picture now opens with its first piece, what is still to come stands as a pale outline from the first frame and fills in on its word, the big numbers carry a picture (a bucket over $10, a ticket over $11.31, a coin over 48¢ and 30¢), and the counter's bucket is the same real-looking popcorn as the thumbnail. Measured: the longest nearly empty stretch went from 3.4 s (v1) to 0.2 s, at a cut.

Built for this video: the cinema auditorium (seats, the screen, the smell pipe; used in part 2); a scene now shows only the things the script lists; a price tag takes words as long as CHEAP PRINTER; a number that counts up is there from the start of its shot and lands on its value as the narrator says it, so no shot waits empty.
The money split of the snack dollar is drawn with the cinema's 82 cents first, so the big share fills the top of the bar as in every split; the words are as written.
notes: Biku's script, used word for word (as-is); every picture is the one he wrote after each line, its pieces arriving on the words he named. Looked at as frames across the opening: the machine on 'cinema', the bucket on 'popcorn', the hand with $10 on 'ten'. The self-check cuts no strips for explainer graphics (it follows people), so the whole part was looked at two frames a second by hand: no picture opens empty; the pale outlines of the coming pieces (the queue, the film studio box, the second bar) read as shapes still to fill, not as mistakes.

Checked against the sources: $11.31 (The Numbers, 2025); 48.1% of admissions to film costs (AMC 2025, whole company); $8.57 snacks per visitor and about 18.1% food and drink costs (AMC 2025, US). The CNN, ABC and KTLA figures are as given in his script.
The narrator is the studio's placeholder voice (Kokoro): no voice has been picked for What's the Catch? yet.
Claude cannot hear: the voice, the music and the few sounds need Biku's ears.
